description:
¡Hola! Somos el equipo de la Universidad Santo Tomás Seccional Tunja (Santoto) participando en el NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Afrontamos el reto "Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map" para crear una herramienta de navegación interactiva para astronautas en Marte usando datos de la NASA.

Buscamos compañeros apasionados en: • Software / Programación • Análisis de Datos • Diseño UI/UX

¡Únete y construyamos el futuro desde Tunja!
summary:
Marswalk HUD is a web-based heads-up display that helps astronauts plan and survive a walk on the surface of Mars. It combines real NASA data into a single go / no-go decision: orbital imagery and terrain from Mars Trek (CTX, HiRISE, THEMIS, MOLA), rover traverse elevations, weather from Perseverance’s MEDA station, regional geology from USGS, and space-weather alerts from NASA DONKI.

Users explore Mars in 15° blocks to see which data exists, then choose one of three developed zones: Jezero, Gale or Mount Sharp. For each route, the HUD simulates oxygen, battery, radiation dose and slope at every step, and checks terrain, daylight, duration, dust, radiation, hazards and walk-back distance against NASA’s Artemis III suit limits. Crews can change conditions, mark hazards on the map, and instantly see the verdict update.

It matters because surviving another planet depends on turning scattered scientific data into clear, fast, life-critical decisions.
details:
What it does and how it works
MarsWalk Map answers the “Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map” challenge with a helmet visor for planning and carrying out a walk on Mars. Its global view splits the planet into 15° × 15° blocks and reports how many of six data types each one has. Three zones are fully built: a 1.8 km route along Jezero’s delta front, 1.2 km from Bradbury Landing to Yellowknife Bay in Gale, and 2.2 km across the boxwork formations of Mount Sharp. Along each route, segments turn green, yellow or red by slope, and the HUD tracks the next target, distance, heading, oxygen, battery, time and dose. A traffic-light verdict weighs terrain, light, duration, dust, radiation, hazards and load, and the app verifies that the farthest point stays within 1.38 km of base, NASA’s walk-back limit for Artemis III.
github.com
Benefits and intended impact
Crews get one clear go / no-go answer instead of scattered datasets. They can flag extra hazards themselves, share gear weight between two suits or hand it to a cargo rover, and immediately see the consequences. Every stop also teaches: it shows a real rover photo, the science findings and the task to do there.
github.com
Tools and data
We wrote it in HTML, CSS and JavaScript with the Leaflet map library, hosted on GitHub Pages; nothing needs to be installed. NASA Trek’s WMTS service supplies the Viking, MOLA, THEMIS, CTX and HiRISE maps, while routes and elevations come from Perseverance and Curiosity waypoint files. MEDA and REMS provide weather, NASA DONKI provides space weather, USGS provides geology, and Curiosity’s RAD provides the radiation reference.
github.com
Creativity
We borrowed the drag-to-compare layer slider from NASA Worldview and put it inside an astronaut’s visor. The page switches fully between English and Spanish and adapts to tablets and phones.
github.com
What we considered
Honesty about data came first. Our documentation separates what is real from what is assumed: maps, routes, elevations, photos and weather are real, whereas dust, oxygen and battery are simple controls or models. Only hazards documented by NASA appear by default. We also state our limits: the route retraces the rover’s actual path and is not computed by an algorithm.
